\subsubsection{Coverage and Bandwidth}\label{sss:eis-coverage}

At the measured excitation the channel covers \SI{236}{\ohm} to
\SI{14.79}{\mega\ohm}, \num{4.80} decades (Table~\ref{tab:eis-coverage}). Each
gain code spans \(639\times\), \num{2.81} decades, between the impedance at
which the excitation's peak current fills the \(\pm\SI{0.80}{\volt}\) compliance
and the impedance at which the fundamental of the output falls to one converter
code. Adjacent codes overlap by more than a decade, so \textbf{there are no
impedance seams}: the 320-tap ladder tiles that span as a continuum, and the
only seams in the sweep are the ladder's own carry codes
(Section~\ref{ss:tiarprog}), which move a window edge by far less than the
overlap. The frequency and impedance limits do not collide either --- a
capacitive interface's impedance falls as frequency rises, so a sweep walks down
the table as it walks up in frequency, and the high-gain codes whose feedback
pole sits between \num{3.7} and \SI{11}{\kilo\hertz} are only selected at the
low-frequency end. That pole is measured here and confirms the
\SI{22}{\pico\farad} compensation capacitor to better than \SI{1}{\percent}:
\SI{52.0}{\kilo\hertz} against \SI{52.2}{\kilo\hertz} predicted at gain code 20,
\SI{3.75}{\kilo\hertz} against \SI{3.76}{\kilo\hertz} at code 319.

\textbf{The capacitor is confirmed; the pole is not a constant.} It moves by
\(\pm\SI{1.2}{\percent}\) over the corner set, which holds the poly at typical,
and by \SIrange{2.40}{6.61}{\kilo\hertz} at code 319 once the poly is cornered
too --- because the pole is \(1/2\pi R_f C_F\) and \(R_f\) is an
\SI{11}{\percent} process quantity (Section~\ref{sss:eis-accuracy}). The window
itself translates with \(R_f\) for the same reason: it holds to
\SIrange{232}{243}{\ohm} and \SIrange{14.58}{14.98}{\mega\ohm} over the corner
set, \numrange{4.79}{4.81} decades everywhere, but a poly-cornered die runs from
\SI{158}{\ohm} to \SI{20.0}{\mega\ohm}. Every tap is the same poly, so the span
is unchanged and one dc calibration recovers the absolute edges.

\paragraph{The band edge is a phase specification, not a magnitude one.}
Presenting each gain code with a pure resistor of exactly \(R_f/40\) freezes the
noise gain across the sweep and measures the edge directly. The dc error then
scales exactly with that ratio --- \num{0.120}, \num{0.330}, \num{0.660},
\SI{1.322}{\percent} at \num{7.3}, \num{20}, \num{40}, \num{80} --- so the form
of the design equation holds, and it holds across corners too, at
\SIrange{0.52}{0.92}{\percent} about the nominal \SI{0.660}{\percent} at ratio
\num{40}, with only the amplifier's open-loop gain moving. Its bandwidth
prediction does not hold: the \(\pm\SI{1}{\percent}\) magnitude edge measures
\SIrange{9.1}{22.7}{\kilo\hertz} across the gain codes against
\SI{5.56}{\kilo\hertz} predicted, \num{1.6} to \(4\times\) pessimistic, while the
\(\pm\SI{0.573}{\degree}\) phase edge measures \SIrange{5.53}{6.93}{\kilo\hertz}
--- the predicted value. The same model under-predicts the error itself by
\SI{42}{\percent} where the noise gain is near unity (\num{0.029} measured
against \(0.021\,\%\)), which at that size changes nothing.

\paragraph{The band holds across corners, and the phase gate stays the binding
one.} Repeating the fixed-ratio measurement over the seven corner points moves
the phase gate by \SI{-4.3}{\percent} at worst
(Table~\ref{tab:eis-band-corner}): \SI{5.29}{\kilo\hertz} at the slow corner
against \SI{5.53}{\kilo\hertz} nominal, and \SIrange{5.29}{7.53}{\kilo\hertz}
over every corner and gain code. The magnitude edge spans
\SIrange{8.4}{27.1}{\kilo\hertz} against \SIrange{9.1}{22.7}{\kilo\hertz}
nominal, its minimum at \SI{85}{\celsius} and gain code 102, still
\(1.6\times\) above the phase gate at that worst point. \textbf{At nominal poly
the usable band is therefore \SI{0.1}{\hertz} to \SI{5.3}{\kilo\hertz} set by
phase}, with magnitude in specification to at least \SI{8.4}{\kilo\hertz} --- a
conclusion the corners make firmer, since the two gates are worst at opposite
ends of the set.

\paragraph{Freezing the noise gain does not freeze the band edge.} With the poly
ladder and the metal--insulator--metal capacitor cornered as well, the phase
edge at the bottom gain code runs \SIrange{3.40}{10.36}{\kilo\hertz} at a frozen
ratio of \num{40}, and \SIrange{2.52}{15.36}{\kilo\hertz} for a fixed
calibration resistor sized from the nominal \(R_f\) --- a factor of three and a
factor of six on a headline specification. \textbf{The frozen ratio protects the
dc error and not the edge.} It protects the dc error exactly: scaling each
cornered run's error by the ratio it actually achieved reproduces the
frozen-ratio value to three digits, \(0.484\,\% \times 40/26.9 = 0.719\,\%\)
against \(0.720\,\%\) measured and \(0.706\,\% \times 40/54.0 = 0.523\,\%\)
against \(0.523\,\%\). The edge is set by the feedback pole instead, and the
pole is a poly and capacitor quantity: it moves \(1.77\times\) and
\(0.64\times\) where \(R_f\) alone moves \(1.50\times\) and \(0.74\times\).
\textbf{Under that caveat the usable band is \SI{2.52}{\kilo\hertz}} and the
\(\pm\SI{1}{\percent}\) magnitude edge \SIrange{5.9}{37.6}{\kilo\hertz}, still
at least \(1.6\times\) above the phase gate everywhere, so the band stays a
phase specification. The fast and slow passive sections sit at about
\(\pm3\sigma\) of the process spread of Section~\ref{sss:eis-accuracy}: that
\SI{2.52}{\kilo\hertz} is a worst-case die, not a typical one.
